changelog_text:
A shared world for Kitten Space Agency: several players, each in their own game, flying in
one universe kept by a dedicated server that runs on Linux with no game installed.

Everyone in a world needs **KSA `2026.11.10.5801`** and a mod of this release. A game and a
server speaking different versions refuse each other by name rather than misread the
bytes, and this one speaks **protocol 23**.

## What's new

Another player's craft is where it is. A copy was drawn 150 ms in the past,
which is how a walking thing is drawn smoothly and in low orbit is a kilometre:
a craft was put back a kilometre the instant its engine lit, a kitten out of a
hatch appeared a kilometre behind its capsule, and two players in orbit were
never beside each other. A copy is drawn at the present now. Two craft meeting
in orbit are drawn 12-14 mm from where their owners have them, and that over a
wire holding every datagram 50 ms give or take 20 and losing one in fifty.

You can dock with a craft nobody is flying. The two become one craft for
everyone, and two again when you undock. Two players' craft do not dock yet: the
ports touch, nothing happens, and you are told why.

A warp climbs to its speed. Asked for 1000x, the world ran at 1000x for a second
before any machine could say it could not keep up and then spent nineteen
seconds making that up, and when a long warp ended, the game that had run least
far ahead set the clock and the other stood still for the difference: two and a
half minutes, once. A warp now starts a step above normal and climbs as far as
every machine in the room can fly, a room that is catching up is left at the
speed it is catching up at, and when the warp ends the clock goes on to the game
that ran furthest. A game that is at no craft keeps the room's time, where it
came back from a 50x warp 229 s behind everybody.

A crash is the same crash in both games. A craft that dropped a stage or lost a
part vanished from every other game for five seconds; it changes shape in one
frame. Wreckage was drawn metres from where it was and jumping, ten to twenty
times a crash by a metre or more; a rocket falling over into thirty pieces now
has its worst piece within two metres and none that jumps. Pieces that stood in
their maker's world and no other, three of twenty-eight, are in both. And a
craft somebody was watching as it docked or crashed could be taken by the
watcher in the frame it left, and rebuilt in every world inside what it had
become part of. It is not taken.

A kitten walking was drawn further behind itself every second of the walk, to
1.6 m, and caught up in jumps. It is drawn 4-5 cm behind.

Four things were said once, and a wire that loses one datagram in fifty showed
what each cost: a game in a world the server did not count it in, a server
waiting for good on a world it had asked nobody for, a warp still shown after it
had ended, and a destroyed craft standing on in every world but its owner's.
Each is said until it has been heard.

For whoever runs a server. `--trace <path>` writes the clock and the warp a line
of JSON at a time, for a test and for nothing else. And from 0.16.1, which was
never tagged and is all in this release: an advertising server reads
`directories.txt` for itself once an hour and withdraws from any directory that
has left it, so it now contacts raw.githubusercontent.com, which an egress
allowlist holding only a directory's address will refuse; a server that cannot
read the list announces where 0.16.0 did. That list has a second directory in
it, `ksamp.safeshows.dev`.

Not right yet. A craft nobody owns is left to each world, and after a long warp
one stood 3.4 m from itself in two games, so one player saw a docking 3.4 m from
the port. A piece of wreckage at rest that gets struck is drawn metres out for
its last second or two. All of this was measured with two games on one machine,
on loopback and through a relay that delays and drops; what two games across the
internet do is still not known.

Nothing in the protocol changed: 0.16 and 0.17 speak version 23 and can play
together. A game still on 0.16 draws everybody else as 0.16 did.

<details>
<summary>Every change since v0.16.0</summary>

- docs: a day of two games measured, and what the handoff now says to do
- test(tools): both games recorded a frame at a time, and a warp walked and judged
- feat(mod): the bridge points a craft, lands it on its engine and flies it onto a port
- fix(mod): a copy stays with its craft through a walk, a breakup and a docking
- feat(server): --trace writes the clock and the warp a line at a time
- fix(server): a warp climbs to its speed, and what was said once is said again
- fix(protocol): another player's craft is drawn where it is now
- docs: a handoff for testing multiplayer with two games
- docs: the warp stop, the wire, and a kitten that does not arrive whole
- feat(server): a relay that holds datagrams, for testing off loopback
- fix(server): the clock keeps up with a room that has run past it
- docs: half a minute of warp costs eight minutes of frozen game
- docs: ending a timewarp stops the room, and a plan for testing the clock
- docs: a lone player warped past the server and his game stopped dead
- docs: what two games can be made to do, and what they cannot
- test(tools): the breakup run measures what it claims to
- feat(mod): the bridge starts a game, builds a craft and fails its parts
- fix(mod): wreckage is somebody's craft in both worlds
- chore: a second directory joins the shared list
- feat(server): an advertising server reads the shared directory list
- docs: the documentation says what the code does
- docs: running a directory says the easy ways first
</details>

## Playing

Install [StarMap](https://github.com/StarMapLoader/StarMap), unzip `KSAMultiplayer-*.zip`
into KSA's `mods` folder and enable it. The **PLAY MULTIPLAYER** window comes up before
anything else: pick a server from the list it shows, or type an address, and press
**CONNECT**.

There is a server at **`mp.ksarmory.com`** to try it on.

Hold **Tab** for who is playing and their ping, **Enter** for a chat line. A craft someone
else is flying carries their name and is theirs: you can watch it, not fly it. Changing the
simulation speed is put to everyone first, and only whoever asked can end the warp.

## Hosting

```bash
docker run -dit --name ksamp -p 50100:50100/udp -v ksamp-world:/data \
    -e KSAMP_NAME="My server" ghcr.io/laurensdev/ksamp-server@sha256:e81f7f9722995635ff3a67789780cb6790ac8f654745eaa211c57f9a1c93eb74
```

Or an executable from below, needing no .NET and no KSA:
`ksamp-server-linux-x64.tar.gz` (with a systemd unit beside it),
`ksamp-server-linux-arm64.tar.gz` for a Pi or an ARM VPS, or
`ksamp-server-win-x64.zip` to run `ksamp-server.exe` on the machine you already have.
The server has no world until a player gives it one, and hands that world to everyone who
joins after -- or set `empty-world` and it starts with one of its own.

Hosting on the same machine you play on works: the server is its own process and needs no
game. Whoever else joins needs the port open to them.

Its commands are typed into its console, which is standard input -- hence `-it` above, and
`docker attach ksamp` to reach it, Ctrl+P Ctrl+Q to leave it running. `clear` is the broom
for a world filling up with spent stages: every craft nobody is flying goes, out of every
game and not just out of the server, and `clear Rocket_*` narrows it. `reload` hands the
world out again, which takes a few seconds and no reconnection, and is the only thing that
ever puts universe time back.

## Upgrading a server when KSA has

A world remembers the KSA build of whoever gave it to the server, and the server turns away
anyone running a different one. So the day KSA updates, a world seeded before it refuses
**everybody who updates** -- and nothing says so from inside the game beyond the refusal.
Either `fresh` at the console, which throws that world away and starts an empty one, or
`set ksa-build <the new build>` to make the operator's word the test instead of the
world's. A world the server started by itself records no build and turns nobody away.

## State

Two games on one machine have flown in one world through it: launching, EVA, chat, the
scoreboard, nametags, a voted time warp, and an 89-part rocket staged while the other game
watched and rebuilt the stage it dropped. Another player's engines are seen to burn even on
a craft this game is not simulating, 7,576 km away. What two games across the internet do
is not known yet.

listing.description:
A shared world for **Kitten Space Agency**: several players, each in their own game, flying in one universe kept by a **dedicated server**. The server runs on Linux, Windows or a Raspberry Pi, needs no copy of the game, and holds the world whether anybody is playing or not.

Any craft syncs: rockets, rovers, kittens walking about on EVA. You see other players fly, stage, burn and crash in real time, each craft carrying its owner's name.

### Playing together

- **A craft is its owner's.** You can watch one somebody else is flying, ride along with it, and see its engines burn — but not take it, board it or empty it out. When its owner leaves, it comes free.
- **One clock.** Everybody keeps the server's time. A game that falls behind catches up on its own, and nobody is left watching a world minutes out of date.
- **Time warp is asked, not taken.** Changing the simulation speed is put to the room first, and only whoever asked can end it. A game that cannot keep up holds the speed down for everyone, so nothing runs away from the slowest machine.
- **Hold Tab** for who is playing and their ping, **Enter** for a chat line.
- Launchpads are shared out, so two players launching at one site do not land on top of each other.

### The server

One self-contained executable. Point it at a port and it waits; the first player to join gives it their world, and it hands that world to everyone who joins after. Or set `empty-world` and it starts with an empty one of its own, so nobody has to seed it.

It keeps the world between runs, saves periodically, and has a console: `clear` sweeps up the spent stages a shared world fills with, `reload` hands the world out again without anybody reconnecting, and `fresh` throws it away and starts over. Players can be made admins and run those commands from inside the game.

There is a server at **`mp.ksarmory.com`** to try it on.

### What you need

Everyone in a world needs **the same KSA build**, the same mod version, and every mod the world's craft use. The server turns away anyone who differs and says what is missing, rather than letting a mismatch corrupt the world quietly.

### Honest status

Two games on one machine have flown in one world through all of this: launching, EVA, chat, nametags, a voted warp, and an 89-part rocket staged while the other game watched and rebuilt the dropped stage as its own craft. Another player's engines are seen to burn even on a craft your game is not simulating, thousands of kilometres away.

What a dozen players across the internet do to it is not known yet. Bug reports are welcome.
